title: The sower (Matthew 13:1–9)
hookLine: seed lands on path, rock, thorns and good soil; most is wasted, and the harvest is huge anyway
tomorrow: The mustard seed and the yeast (Matthew 13:31–33)

cards: A farmer walks the edge of his field, a bag of seed on his hip. He takes a handful and flings it in a wide arc. He isn't placing seeds.
He's throwing. Some lands on the hard footpath, and the birds have it before he finishes the row. Some lands where rock sits under a skin of soil: it shoots up fast, and the first hot day kills it.
Some lands among thorns and gets strangled. And some lands in good ground. Plenty of the listeners had done this with their own hands.
They knew how much seed a farmer loses. They didn't expect the ending.

teach.h: A SOWER WENT FORTH TO SOW
teach.b: It opens, in the King James: "Behold, a sower went forth to sow."

teach.h: THREE GROUNDS OUT OF FOUR FAIL
teach.b: Three kinds of ground out of four fail. Keep count and it's a story about waste.

Then the last line: the good ground "brought forth fruit, some an hundredfold, some sixtyfold, some thirtyfold." Some readers hear a hundredfold as the kind of number that makes a farmer laugh out loud.
Everyone knew about failure. The surprise is a harvest that dwarfs it. Later in the same chapter, the Gospel gives an explanation, told to the disciples.
The seed is the word, the good news of God's kingdom. The grounds are kinds of listeners: one hears and loses it at once, one is thrilled for a week, one lets worries choke it, one lets it grow.
Christians hear the story from two sides, sometimes both at once.
About the sower: keep throwing, even when most of it seems wasted, because you can't see where the good ground is. About the soil: what kind of ground am I, today?
And notice: the farmer doesn't test the soil or save his seed for the good patch.
He throws it on path, rock and thorns, as if there's plenty to go around. It ends: "Who hath ears to hear, let him hear." The story stops, and hands the question to you.

how: The parable of the sower is told in Matthew, Mark and Luke and read aloud in churches; Christians hear it as a question about how they receive the word, and as encouragement to keep sharing it.

games.q: you're a farmer with a bag of seed. you can see the path, the rocks and the thorns. what do you do?
o: throw it everywhere, on all of it.
games.why: the sower in the story throws everywhere, on path, rock and thorns. most of it is lost, and the harvest is still a hundredfold.

practice: Let your breathing slow, and picture the four grounds: the hard path, too trampled to take anything in; thin soil over rock; the thorns, plenty of life but the worries winning; the good earth, open and ready.
Without grading yourself, notice which one you are today. It's only today: ground changes, paths get broken up, thorns get pulled, so let yourself be whatever ground you are.

wordCard.voice: The sower. A farmer throwing seed everywhere, as if there's plenty, and a harvest that dwarfs the waste.

orig.note: Greek: "the one sowing," from speirō, to scatter seed.
